name: Clavicular's looksmaxxing philosophy
summary: The aggressive 'ascension' approach promoted by streamer Clavicular, spanning steroids, peptides and bonesmashing talk, with heavy criticism from medical sources.
lead: Clavicular is the online alias of Braden Eric Peters, an American influencer born in December 2005 and raised in Hoboken, New Jersey, who gained prominence through livestreams and clips on Kick and TikTok in 2025 and 2026 . He promotes looksmaxxing, a trend of methods for improving appearance, and is associated with more extreme 'ascension' practices .

name: Looksmax.org / forum participation
summary: The main forum hub of looksmaxxing culture, where members post progress photos, seek PSL ratings and swap guides.
lead: Looksmax.org is an online forum that Grokipedia describes as one of the main later hubs of looksmaxxing, together with forum.looksmaxxing.com, hosting guides, PSL rating threads and rate-me requests . Looksmaxxing, a practice focused on maximising male attractiveness, formed on incel-linked message boards in the 2010s, and Wikipedia names PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net as the 'PSL forums' that created the PSL rating scale .

name: Dopamine / porn avoidance
summary: Abstaining from porn, masturbation or other stimulation to 'reset' dopamine, popular in self-improvement circles; claimed benefits lack supporting evidence per researchers.
lead: Dopamine and porn avoidance refers to abstaining from pornography, masturbation and other stimulating behaviours in order to improve self-control, mood or perceived attractiveness. Two overlapping movements are involved: NoFap, an online community founded in June 2011 by Alexander Rhodes after a Reddit thread, and dopamine fasting, developed by psychologist Cameron Sepah as a cognitive behavioural tool .
claims: Abstaining resets dopamine and increases confidence, focus and attractiveness

name: Alpha / sigma male frameworks
summary: Informal alpha/beta/sigma ranking of men, borrowed from animal behavior; popular online, not an established model of human society.
lead: Alpha, beta and sigma male frameworks are informal typologies that sort men into social ranks, usually in online men's communities such as the manosphere, pickup-artist circles and looksmaxxing forums. "Alpha" denotes a dominant, high-status man, "beta" a lower-status or deferential one, and "sigma" a solitary, high-status "lone wolf" who operates outside the hierarchy. The terms are borrowed from animal-behavior research on mating access, territory and feeding order.

name: Social proof / status maxxing
summary: Raising perceived status through social signals; the psychology of social proof is well established, the looksmaxxing tactics are untested.
lead: Social proof, as a looksmaxxing concept, refers to using signals of other people's approval, such as followers, friends, group photos, endorsements and association with high-status people, to raise perceived status and attractiveness. "Status maxxing" is the related idea of improving one's rank in social hierarchies alongside, or instead of, physical appearance.

name: Money maxxing / career maxxing
summary: The idea that income and career success can offset or replace looks; supported in part by mate-preference research, untested as a strategy.
lead: Money maxxing and career maxxing describe the idea in looksmaxxing and manosphere communities that income, wealth and professional success can compensate for, or substitute for, physical attractiveness. It is often presented as an alternative route to status for men who consider their looks fixed.

name: Smile practice / smile maxxing
summary: Training a more natural, appealing smile; smile perception research exists, but smile training itself is unstudied.
lead: Smile practice, or smile maxxing, is the practice of training one's smile, often in a mirror, to look more natural, symmetrical or attractive. Community discussion focuses on the difference between a polite and a genuine smile and on how smiling is perceived.

name: Posture / frame / body language
summary: Open, upright body language to look and feel more confident; feelings effects hold up, hormone and behavior claims do not replicate well.
lead: In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities, "posture", "frame" and "body language" refer to how a person holds and moves the body, with the belief that upright, open and expansive postures make a person look and feel more confident and attractive. "Power posing" is a closely related and widely publicised version.

name: Photo comparison / flip test
summary: Comparing a face with its mirror image to judge looks; related to mere exposure, but the method itself is untested.
lead: The photo comparison or flip test is a looksmaxxing practice in which a person compares photos of themselves with their mirror image, or flips a photo horizontally, to judge which version looks better or to understand why they look different in pictures than in the mirror.

name: Mirror flip / symmetry test
summary: Flip your photo and compare the halves; symmetry matters in attractiveness research, but this self-test itself is unvalidated.
lead: The mirror flip or symmetry test is a self-assessment practice in which a person compares a photograph of their face with its left-right reversed copy, or compares the two halves of the face, to judge how symmetrical it looks. It belongs to the facial-analysis side of looksmaxxing, where symmetry is one of several features people assess.

name: Facial analysis YouTube channels
summary: Creators rate faces on feature scales like PSL; popular in the scene, unvalidated, and linked by press to body-image concerns.
lead: Facial analysis content is video and livestream material in which creators assess faces, rating features such as eye shape, jawline and cheeks, often against community scales like the PSL scale. It is a staple of looksmaxxing culture online.

name: Anti-looksmax / 'touch grass' critiques
summary: The counter-discourse: journalists and researchers criticize looksmaxxing, while 'touch grass' is the informal version.
lead: Critiques of looksmaxxing come from journalists, researchers, clinicians and others who argue the practice is harmful or misguided; a common informal version tells practitioners to 'touch grass', a phrase meaning go outside, used mockingly at people who seem absorbed in online content.

name: Therapy for looks-related anxiety (ACT)
summary: A mindfulness-based therapy sometimes suggested for appearance anxiety; well studied generally, untested for looksmaxxing.
lead: Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) is a form of cognitive behavioral therapy that uses mindfulness to help people notice thoughts and feelings, accept them rather than fight them, and commit to actions based on personal values. In looksmaxxing discussions it is raised as a psychological approach to appearance-related anxiety.

name: Antidepressants / anxiety meds
summary: Rx mental-health drugs used for anxiety and depression; not appearance treatments, with modest effects and real side effects.
lead: Antidepressants are prescription drugs used mainly for major depressive disorder and also for anxiety disorders such as generalized and social anxiety, panic disorder, OCD and PTSD. Main classes include SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics and MAOIs.

name: Psychedelic therapy for self-image
summary: Experimental idea of using psychedelics for body image; no direct studies, and the drugs are controlled substances.
lead: Psychedelic therapy is the proposed use of drugs such as psilocybin, LSD and MDMA in mental health treatment, usually with preparation and integration sessions. Its use for self-image is an experimental idea; research has focused on depression, PTSD, anxiety and substance use.

name: Social media dysmorphia (filter dysmorphia / Snapchat dysmorphia)
summary: Informal name for wanting to look like your filtered selfie; linked in studies to body dissatisfaction and surgery interest, but not a formal diagnosis.
lead: Social media dysmorphia, also called Snapchat dysmorphia, filter dysmorphia or selfie dysmorphia, is an informal term for the phenomenon of people seeking cosmetic procedures to resemble their filtered or edited selfies, or feeling distress at the gap between their real appearance and edited images of themselves. It is not a formal diagnosis. Clinicians discuss it in relation to body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), an obsessive preoccupation with perceived flaws in appearance.

name: Beauty privilege research (pretty premium)
summary: Economic research finding that better-looking people earn and get hired somewhat more; effect sizes and causes are debated.
lead: The 'pretty premium' or beauty premium refers to the finding, reported in labour-economics and psychology research, that people rated as more physically attractive tend to receive better outcomes in hiring and pay than people rated as less attractive. The idea is often called 'pretty privilege' or 'lookism' in popular and online usage.

name: Evolutionary psychology of attractiveness
summary: The theory that beauty preferences are evolved mate-choice adaptations; often cited online, with mixed and contested support in research.
lead: The evolutionary psychology of attractiveness is the study of human beauty preferences as products of natural and sexual selection. Evolutionary psychology treats the mind as made of specialised mechanisms shaped to solve recurring ancestral problems, including choosing mates. Within this framework, researchers have proposed that preferences for features such as facial symmetry, averageness, sexual dimorphism and particular body ratios evolved because they signalled health, fertility or genetic quality.

name: Spreader grafts
summary: Cartilage strips placed beside the septum to open the internal nasal valve and keep the nose bridge straight after hump reduction; supported mainly by surgeon case series.
lead: Spreader grafts are thin strips of cartilage, usually taken from the nasal septum, that surgeons place between the septum and the upper lateral cartilages during rhinoplasty. They are used to widen the internal nasal valve, support or straighten the middle third of the nose, and keep the dorsal aesthetic lines smooth after a dorsal hump has been reduced .

name: Columellar strut graft
summary: A hidden cartilage post under the nasal tip that supports it; surgeons debate how much it raises the tip and compare it with septal extension grafts.
lead: A columellar strut graft is a piece of cartilage placed between the medial crura of the lower lateral cartilages in the columella, the strip of tissue between the nostrils, during rhinoplasty to support the nasal tip. Surgeons describe it as a popular form of invisible graft because it is hidden beneath the skin .

name: Rib cartilage rhinoplasty
summary: Nose surgery that uses rib cartilage for large structural grafts, mainly in major reconstruction and revisions; evidence is limited to small surgeon series.
lead: Rib cartilage rhinoplasty is nose surgery in which cartilage harvested from the patient's rib (costal cartilage) is used for structural grafts. General references note that septal cartilage is the preferred graft source and that rib or ear cartilage is used when septal cartilage is insufficient .

name: Rhinoplasty tip-narrowing sutures
summary: Stitches that reshape the cartilage of a wide nasal tip during rhinoplasty; sources found here are sparse.
lead: Tip-narrowing sutures are stitches placed in the lower lateral cartilages of the nose during rhinoplasty to reshape and narrow a broad or bulbous tip without removing cartilage. General rhinoplasty references describe sutures as a way to narrow a wide tip by tightening the folded cartilage apex .

name: Deep plane facelift
summary: A facelift that lifts skin and SMAS together as one unit with ligament release for the jawline, midface and neck; evidence is mostly surgeon series.
lead: A deep plane facelift is a facelift technique in which the surgeon dissects beneath the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) and repositions the skin and SMAS together as a single composite flap. Descriptions of the extended version emphasize release of facial retaining ligaments so the flap can be moved to volumize the midface and the jawline .

name: SMAS plication facelift
summary: A facelift that folds and sutures the SMAS layer for a limited lift; less invasive than deep plane, with moderate effect.
lead: SMAS plication is a facelift approach in which the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS), the fibromuscular layer beneath the facial skin, is folded and sutured to tighten it, with little or no extensive dissection of the layer. General references describe it as giving moderate tightening and being less invasive, but with limited mobilization compared with SMAS flap or deep-plane techniques .

name: Composite facelift
summary: A deep facelift that lifts skin, SMAS and the orbicularis muscle as one unit, reaching up to the lower eyelid and cheek junction; evidence is surgeon-series level.
lead: The composite facelift is a surgical rhytidectomy technique that elevates the skin, the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) and the orbicularis oculi muscle together, extending into the periorbital region to address descent of the midface and the lower eyelid to cheek junction. It is described as a modification of the deep-plane facelift.

name: Subperiosteal facelift
summary: A midface lift done beneath the periosteum, often endoscopically, that repositions cheek tissue vertically; documented mainly in surgeon series from the 1990s onward.
lead: A subperiosteal facelift is a surgical technique in which the soft tissues of the face are lifted completely off the underlying bone by dissecting beneath the periosteum, then repositioned. It is used to address deep nasolabial folds and sagging cheeks and is often combined with other techniques.

name: Mini facelift (S-lift)
summary: A short-scar facelift using small incisions near the ear, usually without neck work; lighter recovery, and Wikipedia describes the result as more temporary.
lead: The mini facelift is a family of short-scar rhytidectomy techniques, commonly called the S-lift, that use limited incisions and omit the neck lift. Wikipedia says it suits people with deep nasolabial folds and sagging but a firm, well-contoured neck, has less downtime, and may be done endoscopically; it describes the result as more temporary.

name: MACS lift
summary: A short-scar facelift that hangs the lower and mid face from above with purse-string sutures along a purely vertical vector; surgeon series report quicker recovery.
lead: The minimal access cranial suspension (MACS) lift is a short-scar rhytidectomy for the lower and middle third of the face that uses a vertical vector, involves no lateral tension, and in its authors' description can be performed under local anesthesia in 2 to 2.5 hours. It was proposed in 2002 as a modified version of the S-lift, suspending tissue with purse-string sutures.

name: APTOS thread lift
summary: A non-surgical lift using barbed non-absorbable threads placed under the skin; early series report improvement, while case reports document migration and expulsion.
lead: APTOS threads are barbed non-absorbable sutures, originally made of polypropylene with dents along their length, used to lift ptotic facial tissue without a facelift. The technique was described in 2002 by a group who used them in 186 patients and reported success in lifting various areas and improving facial contour.

name: Lower facelift with neck lift
summary: A combined jowl-and-neck lift, often adding platysma work and fat removal to the facelift; literature is surgeon-reported with limited comparative data.
lead: A lower facelift with neck lift is a combined surgical approach to the jowls, jawline and neck, in which facelift tightening of the SMAS or deeper tissues is performed together with treatment of neck structures such as the platysma muscle and submental fat. Wikipedia notes that a traditional facelift addresses neck skin and platysma laxity.
